clue.text: Reprimand man on board for being a ladies' man

parts.note: to carpet someone is to call them in and scold them
a chess piece shaped like a horse's head is one of the men on a chessboard

explanation.surface: A womaniser gets hauled up and told off by a colleague on the company board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'man on board' suggests a company director, but the board is a chessboard and the man is a chess piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Originally one honoured at court rather than in battle, the phrase came to mean a drawing-room gallant devoted to wooing women.

clue.text: Sporting associates plot to get beaten

parts.note: members of a sports team form a club
a bed is a plot of garden ground for flowers

explanation.surface: Fellow sportsmen conspire to have someone given a thrashing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plot' reads as a conspiracy, but it is a garden plot.
explanation.definitionFit: To be hit repeatedly with a heavy stick is to be battered, the sense of beaten here.

clue.text: A grovelling person, a salesman, with a hat

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative
tile is old slang for a hat

explanation.surface: A fawning travelling salesman turns up wearing a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: TILE as a word for a hat is dated slang, from the way a hat covers the head like a roof tile.
explanation.definitionFit: A creepy, sycophantic toady is figuratively called a crawling cold-blooded creature.

clue.text: Spineless creature -the marrow's defective

indicators.note: something defective is faulty, so these letters are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: the 's stands for 'is', so the letters are just those of these two words

explanation.surface: A gardener complains that the marrow is faulty and has been eaten by a pest.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after 'marrow' is 'is', joining the fodder to 'defective'; 'Spineless' is literal: the creature has no backbone.
explanation.definitionFit: This burrowing soil animal is an invertebrate, having no backbone at all.

clue.text: In a manner of speaking, want to work

indicators.note: says the word that follows is to be heard spoken, giving a word of the same sound

parts.note: to want something is to need it

explanation.surface: Put loosely, someone says they have to have a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a manner of speaking' usually means 'so to say', but here it signals a homophone: the K is silent.
explanation.definitionFit: A baker works dough by pressing and folding it with the hands.

clue.text: Live in, like a nun

definitions.meaning: to occupy a place as one's home
a nun wears the religious robe, so she goes about clothed in it; split into two words the letters say exactly that

explanation.surface: Someone moves in and lives as quietly as a sister in a convent.
explanation.definitionFit: To dwell in or occupy a house; split as two words it means wearing a religious garment, as nuns do.

clue.text: Passing requires some strength and ingenuity

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: To get through an exam calls for a bit of muscle and cleverness.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'Passing requires' as the definition, but 'requires' is only the link joining definition to wordplay; 'Passing' alone means giving over by hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving something across to another person, as in passing the salt to a neighbour.

clue.text: Possibly Southend's antepenultimate game

definitions.meaning: south is one of the four cardinal points of the compass, and an end is the last stage, so the town's name is read as those two words
third from last match in a knockout competition, before the semis and the decider

explanation.surface: Southend United might be playing the third-to-last round of a cup.
explanation.walkthrough: Southend-on-Sea is an English seaside town with a football club, Southend United, so the surface reads as a cup tie.
explanation.definitionFit: In a knockout tournament this round precedes the semis and the deciding match, making it third from the end.

clue.text: Money-lender receives little cash from a man like Stephen

indicators.note: the money-lender takes in the small coin, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: a usurer lends money at extortionate interest
p, a penny, is a small amount of money

explanation.surface: A loan shark takes in a few pence from a fellow named Stephen.
explanation.walkthrough: King Stephen seized the English throne in 1135 from his cousin Matilda, the heir named by Henry I.
explanation.definitionFit: King Stephen took the crown that Henry I had promised to Matilda, so he grabbed power unlawfully.

clue.text: Points he can alter and improve

parts.note: E and N, east and north, are two points of the compass

indicators.note: to alter is to change, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Debating points that he can change to strengthen his case.
explanation.definitionFit: To enhance something is to make it better, to heighten its quality.

clue.text: Recalled a wag misrepresented by author

indicators.note: to misrepresent is to give a distorted picture, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A joker remembered being misquoted by a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Edgar Wallace (1875-1932) was a prolific English thriller writer and co-creator of King Kong.
explanation.definitionFit: A hugely prolific English thriller novelist and playwright of the early twentieth century.

clue.text: Hamlet's snag — a common mistake? Nonsense!

parts.note: Hamlet's 'Ay, there's the rub' uses rub to mean an obstacle or difficulty
bish is British slang for a blunder

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at the idea that Hamlet's problem was an everyday error.
explanation.walkthrough: BISH is informal British for a mistake; 'common' hints at its slangy register as well as its frequency.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation dismissing something as worthless drivel or tosh.

clue.text: Expert takes game losing nothing, striking gently

parts.note: a dab, or dab hand, is an expert

indicators.note: the game drops a letter, so it is removed from the word

parts.note: bingo is a numbers game
O, the figure zero, means nothing

explanation.surface: A skilled player takes on a game, loses without scoring, yet hits softly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing nothing' looks like an unbeaten run, but it means BINGO loses its O.
explanation.definitionFit: Patting something lightly, as when applying ointment with quick light touches.

clue.text: Supply has to last without replenishment, initially

indicators.note: the word for last is taken here without one letter, which is removed

parts.note: to last is to endure, to go on

indicators.note: the first letter of replenishment is taken

explanation.surface: Provisions have to hold out with no restocking at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last' is a verb, not 'final'.
explanation.definitionFit: To endue is an old literary verb meaning to endow or provide with a quality.

clue.text: Gerald's to get reclassified as a veteran

indicators.note: to be reclassified is to be sorted again, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of the name with its s

explanation.surface: Gerald's going to be regraded as an old hand.
explanation.walkthrough: The S of 'Gerald's' is part of the anagram fodder here.
explanation.definitionFit: An old hand, someone with long experience of a job or activity.

clue.text: Damage part of clock mechanism round the edge

indicators.note: one word goes round the other, enclosing it

parts.note: a detent is a catch in a clock's escapement that checks the wheel
a rim is an edge

explanation.surface: A clock repairer finds harm to the movement all around its rim.
explanation.walkthrough: A detent is the catch that locks and releases a clock's wheels; a less familiar word to many solvers.
explanation.definitionFit: Harm or injury, as in acting to someone's loss or disadvantage.

clue.text: Where those near bankruptcy would prefer to be? On the contrary

definitions.text: Where those near bankruptcy would prefer to be?
definitions.meaning: people close to going bust would rather be at a safe distance from that state
a stock phrase of emphatic denial, meaning not at all

explanation.surface: A struggling firm's wishful thinking, followed by a flat contradiction.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means a long way off from the thing just mentioned, and idiomatically 'not at all, quite the opposite'.

clue.text: Race meeting causing great trouble to the army

indicators.note: to trouble something is to disturb it, so these letters are stirred up

parts.note: TA is the Territorial Army, the British volunteer reserve

explanation.surface: A sporting event that causes the soldiers no end of bother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Race meeting' suggests horses, but the races are for boats.
explanation.definitionFit: A series of boat races held as a single event, such as Henley's on the Thames.

clue.text: Sun god, Aurora's other name for an Elizabethan

parts.note: Ra is the Egyptian sun god
Aurora Leigh is the heroine of Elizabeth Barrett Browning's verse novel, so Leigh is her surname

explanation.surface: A sun god and the dawn goddess's other title combine to name a Tudor courtier.
explanation.walkthrough: Aurora suggests the Roman dawn goddess, but it is Aurora Leigh, the title character of a verse novel by Elizabeth Barrett Browning.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Walter, explorer and courtier, was a leading figure at the court of Elizabeth I.

clue.text: 50% of senior officers used to suggest a pause

indicators.note: only half the word is kept, the latter five letters being dropped

parts.note: commanders are senior officers

explanation.surface: Half the top brass were brought in to propose a ceasefire.
explanation.walkthrough: '50% of' keeps the first five of the ten letters of COMMANDERS.
explanation.definitionFit: This punctuation mark tells a reader to take a brief breath between parts of a sentence.

clue.text: Material a doctor injected to cut short a pain in the neck

indicators.note: the letters are put inside the other word as a needle goes into skin
the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a crick is a painful stiffness in the neck
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification

explanation.surface: A physician gives an injection to ease a stiff neck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'injected' and 'cut short' are the two indicators; 'a pain in the neck' is meant literally, a stiff neck, not an annoying person.
explanation.definitionFit: Cambric is a fine white linen or cotton fabric, originally from Cambrai.

clue.text: Such is a husband's status as a. Latin poet, having got it in the right order

indicators.text: having got it in the right order
indicators.note: the letters spelling it in the poet's name are put the other way round

parts.note: Martial was a Roman poet famous for his epigrams

explanation.surface: A Latin poet is sorted out to describe being married.
explanation.walkthrough: In MARTIAL the letters T, I read 'ti'; 'having got it in the right order' moves the T after the I so they read 'it'.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to marriage, the condition a husband is in.

clue.text: Made a fuss when horse fell in the river and died

indicators.note: the horse tumbles into the river, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: the Nile is the great African river
a gee-gee is a child's word for a horse

explanation.surface: Someone complains when a horse tumbled into the river and drowned.
explanation.walkthrough: GG is 'gee-gee', a nursery word for a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: To niggle is to complain fussily about petty details, to carp.

clue.text: Fancy woman, being upset, is under the doctor

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece goes below the other

parts.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor

indicators.note: upset means turned upside down, so in a down clue the word reads upwards

parts.note: Mae is a woman's name

explanation.surface: A man's mistress, distressed, is being treated by the doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy woman' reads as a mistress, but 'Fancy' alone is the definition, as a noun meaning a wish.
explanation.definitionFit: A fancy is a whim or wish, an imagined desire.

clue.text: Deity hasn't got a T? That's wrong

indicators.note: the deity is lacking a letter, so it is removed

parts.note: a god is an immortal

explanation.surface: A god lacking a cup of tea would be quite wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a T' plays on 'a tea'.
explanation.definitionFit: Morally bad, contrary to accepted standards of conduct.

clue.text: Girl, a Latvian, given diamonds

parts.note: a Lett is a native of Latvia
ice is slang for diamonds

explanation.surface: A young woman from Latvia is presented with jewels.
explanation.walkthrough: LETT is an old word for a Latvian.
explanation.definitionFit: Lettice is an old-fashioned female given name.

clue.text: Unpredictable creature infiltrating little by little

indicators.note: the creature gets inside the other word

parts.note: Eric, or, Little by Little is a Victorian school story by F.W. Farrar
a rat is a creature

explanation.surface: An erratic animal sneaks in gradually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little by little' seems to mean gradually, but it is the subtitle of Dean Farrar's 1858 school novel 'Eric, or, Little by Little'.
explanation.definitionFit: Irregular and inconsistent, not following any predictable course.

clue.text: Scientific mail that came for editing

indicators.note: editing a text reworks it, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Technical letters that arrived for revision.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to the study of numbers and quantities, and so precise and exact.
